text:
Predicates:
CanRegisterVote(x) ::: x can register to vote in the United States.
ParticipateElection(x) ::: x can participate in the 2024 United States presidential election.
HasUSCitizenship(x) ::: x has United States citizenship.
HasTaiwaneseCitizenship(x) ::: x has Taiwanese citizenship.
RussianOfficial(x) ::: x is a Russian Federation official.
ManagerAtGazprom(x) ::: x is a manager at Gazprom.
Vladimir(x) ::: x is Vladimir.
Ekaterina(x) ::: x is Ekaterina.
Premises:
∀x (CanRegisterVote(x) → ParticipateElection(x)) ::: Everyone who can register to vote in the United States can participate in the election.
HasUSCitizenship(x) → CanRegisterVote(x) ::: If someone has US citizenship, then they can register to vote.
(HasUSCitizenship(x) ∨ HasTaiwaneseCitizenship(x)) ::: A person either has US or Taiwanese citizenship.
¬(RussianOfficial(x) ∧ HasTaiwaneseCitizenship(x)) ::: No Russian Federation official holds Taiwanese citizenship.
¬(Vladimir(x) ∧ HasTaiwaneseCitizenship(x)) ::: Vladimir neither holds Taiwanese citizenship nor is he a manager at Gazprom.
¬(Vladimir(x) ∧ ManagerAtGazprom(x)) ::: Vladimir is not a manager at Gazprom.
CanRegisterVote(Ekaterina) ∨ RussianOfficial(Ekaterina) ::: Ekaterina can register to vote, or she is a Russian Federation official.
Conclusion:
¬(CanRegisterVote(Ekaterina) ∧ ParticipateElection(Vladimir)) ::: It is not true that Ekaterina can register to vote and Vladimir can participate in the election.
